source: Kevin DeYoung, Daily Doctrine: A One-Year Guide to Systematic Theology (Crossway, 2024)
note: Original paragraph summaries for display use; not verbatim book text.
title: Daily Doctrine

items.title: Theology
items.summary: Christian theology is the disciplined study of God aimed at knowing him, enjoying fellowship with him, and obeying his will. It rests on Scripture as the final authority and employs the mind in service of faith, not pride.

items.title: Systematic Theology
items.summary: Systematic theology organizes what the whole Bible teaches about particular doctrines into a logical topical framework. It complements biblical, historical, and natural theology by arranging revealed truth around key loci for clearer understanding and worship.

items.title: Divisions of Theology
items.summary: Theology may be false, grounded in human opinion alone, or true theology God gives. True theology is either archetypal, God's own self-knowledge, or ectypal, the limited knowledge communicated to creatures, especially in supernatural Scripture required for salvation.

items.title: Religion
items.summary: In Scripture and historic Christianity, religion names the ordered worship, beliefs, and practices by which people relate to God. It can be corrupt or hypocritical, but true religion expresses genuine faith through doctrine, community, and righteous living.

items.title: Science
items.summary: Calling theology a science means Christian doctrine gathers biblical facts and arranges them into a coherent, logically consistent body of knowledge. It treats Scripture as a reliable source of truth about God, not as lifeless data divorced from worship.

items.title: Speculative or Practical?
items.summary: Theology is both speculative and practical: it contemplates God as worthy of knowledge for his own sake and demands faith, love, and obedience. Purely abstract theology or teaching driven only by application both distort the mixed character of sacred doctrine.

items.title: Ad Fontes
items.summary: Ad fontes, meaning to the sources, was a Reformation call to return to primary texts, especially Scripture in its original languages and the writings of antiquity, rather than relying only on layered scholastic commentary.

items.title: Principia
items.summary: Principia are first principles in three senses: the ground of being, the external source of knowledge, and the internal faculty that grasps it. In theology God is the foundation, Scripture the external authority, and faith the internal means of receiving divine truth.

items.title: Faith and Reason
items.summary: Faith and reason serve distinct roles yet cooperate. Reason must not judge God's word by human possibility but instrumentally helps believers understand, deduce, and defend what Scripture teaches. Faith receives revelation; reason organizes it without replacing it.

items.title: Inner Testimony of the Holy Spirit
items.summary: The inner testimony of the Holy Spirit is God's work persuading believers that Scripture is his own word. It does not add new revelation or rest on historical proofs alone but opens hearts to recognize divine authority in the written text.

items.title: Fundamental Articles
items.summary: Fundamental articles are doctrines necessary for saving faith or essential Christian unity, distinguished from secondary matters where believers may disagree. Not every biblical truth carries equal weight; creeds and the gospel core mark what is nonnegotiable.

items.title: Knowing God
items.summary: God makes himself known on his terms through objective revelation, not through rationalism, which makes reason supreme, mysticism, which bypasses Scripture for private impressions, or liberalism, which subordinates doctrine to modern experience.

items.title: Natural Law and Natural Theology
items.summary: Natural law is God's moral standard known through conscience and reason. Natural theology infers truths about the Creator from creation and providence. Both leave sinners without excuse yet cannot reveal saving forgiveness; that requires special revelation in Scripture.

items.title: General Revelation and Special Revelation
items.summary: General revelation is God's disclosure through creation, providence, and conscience, showing his power and moral claims. Special revelation is God's saving word in Scripture, necessary because general revelation cannot teach redemption and the way of eternal life.

items.title: Inspiration
items.summary: Biblical inspiration means all Scripture is God-breathed: the Holy Spirit carried human authors so their writings are fully divine authority and trustworthy communication. Inspiration describes a completed textual fact, not a present feeling readers generate.

items.title: Concursive Operation
items.summary: Concursive inspiration holds that the Spirit so superintended biblical authors that their personalities and styles remained active while the resulting text is entirely God's true word. It rejects dynamic inspiration that allows error and mechanical dictation that erases human agency.

items.title: Perfections of Scripture
items.summary: Scripture's perfections include sufficiency for salvation and godly life, clarity of its central message for believers, final authority over church and conscience, and necessity of the written word after apostolic times. These are often summarized as SCAN.

items.title: Inerrancy
items.summary: Inerrancy holds that Scripture, as God's speech through inspired authors, is wholly true in all it affirms. Because God cannot lie, denying the Bible's reliability impugns either his character or the connection between divine authority and the text.

items.title: The Question of Canon
items.summary: The biblical canon is the fixed collection of sixty-six inspired books, thirty-nine Old Testament and twenty-seven New Testament, recognized as Scripture by Jesus, the apostles, and the church through gradual consensus and formal affirmation.

items.title: Which Books Belong in the Bible?
items.summary: The church did not create biblical authority by vote; it recognized books that bore marks of apostolic origin and divine self-authentication. Canon formation was historical discernment of writings already received as God's word, not ecclesiastical invention of a table of contents.

items.title: The Existence of God
items.summary: Scripture presupposes God's existence as the foundation of all knowledge, while arguments from motion, causation, design, and conscience can support that presupposition. Theism remains a matter of faith, yet rational defense can remove excuses and strengthen believers.

items.title: The Knowability of God
items.summary: God is incomprehensible in the sense that creatures cannot fully exhaust his being, yet he is truly knowable through what he reveals. Sound theology balances divine mystery with real, saving knowledge disclosed in Scripture for faith and obedience.

items.title: Words for God
items.summary: Theologians describe God-talk as analogical: terms like good or wise apply to God and creatures neither with identical meaning nor with unrelated meaning, but with real correspondence qualified by infinite difference.

items.title: The Unity of God
items.summary: The unity of God means his indivisible essence and exclusive sovereignty: one supreme Lord, numerically one in being and without a true peer among all supposed gods or rivals.

items.title: The Spirituality of God
items.summary: God's spirituality means he is immaterial, invisible, and not bound by bodily or spatial limits, yet he is not an abstract force but a substantial personal spirit who knows, wills, and relates to creation.

items.title: The Names of God
items.summary: Biblical names for God reveal his character. Proper names such as El, Elohim, Yahweh, and Kyrios highlight his power, covenant faithfulness, and lordship, inviting worship of the God who defines himself by his revealed titles.

items.title: The Attributes of God
items.summary: Divine attributes are the perfections predicated of God's being, not separate parts added to him. What God has is identical with what he is. Confessions summarize him as eternal, spirit, unchangeable, almighty, wise, holy, and good.

items.title: Incommunicable and Communicable Attributes
items.summary: Incommunicable attributes, such as eternity and infinity, have no true analogue in creatures. Communicable attributes, such as love and mercy, can be reflected in humanity, though only analogically and dependently. The distinction highlights God's otherness and his moral likeness in those made in his image.

items.title: Substance and Accidents
items.summary: In classical terms, accidents are changeable qualities incidental to a substance, which remains what it is without them. God is simple: no attribute is accidental or detachable. Everything true of God is essential to his essence; nothing about him is merely incidental.

items.title: Christian Theology and Greco-Roman Philosophy
items.summary: Christian theology employs Greek philosophical categories to state biblical truth with precision. Scripture remains primary, yet terms such as substance, essence, and person help express monotheism and tri-personhood. The New Testament itself uses metaphysical language that systematic theology develops responsibly.

items.title: The Simplicity of God
items.summary: Divine simplicity means God is not composed of parts or a mixture of attributes. Each perfection is identical with his essence, not a fraction of God ranked above others. God is what he has; no attribute attaches to him from outside.

items.title: Aseity
items.summary: Aseity is God's self-existence: he exists from himself, needs nothing, and depends on no creature. Before creation he was complete. All life derives from him; he never derives being or fulfillment from the world.

items.title: Divine Infinity
items.summary: Divine infinity includes absolute perfection in every attribute, eternity without beginning or succession in God's duration, and immensity beyond spatial limits. Omnipresence stresses his filling all places; immensity stresses that nothing contains him.

items.title: Immutability
items.summary: Immutability means God's essence, knowledge, will, and purposes cannot change for better or worse. He is pure being, not becoming. Because his character is fixed, his promises, justice, and mercy remain utterly reliable.

items.title: Impassibility
items.summary: Impassibility means God's divine nature cannot be acted upon from without or undergo inner change like human passion. Scripture's emotional language toward God is anthropopathic. The Son truly suffered in his human nature in the incarnation; God as God does not.

items.title: Theopaschitism and Patripassianism
items.summary: Theopaschitism wrongly holds that the divine nature itself suffered in Christ's death; patripassianism wrongly holds that the Father suffered with the Son. Both confuse Trinitarian persons and Christ's two natures. Only the incarnate Son endured death in human flesh.

items.title: Attributes of Intellect
items.summary: God's intellectual attributes include omniscience, wisdom, and truthfulness. His knowledge is immediate, exhaustive, and unchanging. His wisdom applies knowledge to ends that glorify him. He is truth itself and cannot lie or contradict his word.

items.title: Attributes of Will
items.summary: God's moral will includes holiness, goodness, love, grace, mercy, patience, and righteousness. He is set apart in purity and always does what is right. Justice and mercy meet at the cross through satisfaction of wrath, not by setting justice aside.

items.title: Attributes of Power
items.summary: Omnipotence is God's unlimited power to accomplish whatever he wills, often through means but never dependent on them. Sovereignty means all events fall under his governing will without nullifying creaturely agency. His power always accords with his goodness and wisdom.

items.title: Transcendence and Immanence
items.summary: Transcendence is God's infinite elevation above creation in holiness, power, and independence. Immanence is his near, personal presence, especially in Christ. Sound doctrine affirms both: a God too great to be domesticated and too good to be distant.

items.title: God as Trinity
items.summary: The Trinity is one God in three eternal persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—sharing one divine essence. It answers who God is beyond his attributes. Historic Christianity treats this as essential to faith, worship, and salvation.

items.title: The Bible and the Trinity
items.summary: Trinitarian doctrine holds that only one God exists; Father, Son, and Spirit are each fully God; and the three persons are not identical. Scripture teaches this pattern through monotheistic texts and passages naming, sending, and equating the three.

items.title: Trinitarian Terms
items.summary: Trinitarian terminology distinguishes persons by eternal relations: the Father unbegotten and begetting, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit proceeding. One divine substance is shared equally. Unity of essence and trinity of persons must neither be blended nor divided.

items.title: One and Three
items.summary: Orthodox Trinitarianism confesses three coequal, coeternal persons in one undivided essence, distinguished by relations of origin. It rejects adoptionism, modalism, Arianism, and tritheism. The persons coinhere without splitting God into three beings or collapsing them into one.

items.title: Eternal Generation
items.summary: Eternal generation is the Father's never-beginning act of communicating the divine essence to the Son, distinguishing persons without creating a second god. The Son is begotten, not made, fully divine and yet not the Father.

items.title: The Filioque Clause
items.summary: Filioque is the Latin for “and the Son,” added at Toledo (589) to the creed’s statement on the Spirit’s procession. The East rejected both the unilateral edit and any threat to the Father’s primacy; Reformed theology affirms double procession from the Father through the Son.

items.title: Perichoresis
items.summary: Perichoresis is the mutual indwelling of Father, Son, and Spirit: each person fully possesses the undivided divine essence while remaining distinct. To know one is to encounter the whole Trinity. This coinherence guards true threeness and true oneness.

items.title: Taxis
items.summary: Trinitarian taxis is orderly relation among persons, not inferior rank. The Father is source; the Son is eternally generated; the Spirit proceeds. Externally, work proceeds from Father through Son in Spirit. Persons share one will and equal glory.

items.title: Inseparable Operations
items.summary: Inseparable operations teach that God's outward works—creation, redemption, providence—proceed from one will shared by Father, Son, and Spirit. Each person acts, yet none works independently or at cross purposes. Scripture may emphasize one person without dividing the action.

items.title: Our Triune God and the Christian Life
items.summary: The Trinity shapes Christian life: creation and new birth are Trinitarian; prayer is to the Father through the Son by the Spirit; eternal love among the persons grounds generous creation. Believers may know each person distinctly in worship and communion.

items.title: The Divine Decrees
items.summary: The divine decrees are God's eternal, single purpose by which he foreordains all that comes to pass for his glory. They are simple, unchangeable, unconditional, and wise. God is not the author of sin, yet even evil acts serve his good design.

items.title: The Will of God
items.summary: God's will is spoken of as decretive (what he ordains and brings to pass) and preceptive (what he commands and delights in). Believers need not discover a hidden roadmap for every decision; revealed moral will calls for holiness, Spirit-led obedience, and conformity to Christ.

items.title: Freedom of the Will
items.summary: After the fall, human willing remains real and voluntary though enslaved to sin; apart from grace no one chooses God, yet sinners stay morally responsible. Divine decree governs all events without making God the author of evil or reducing people to puppets.

items.title: God’s Permission
items.summary: Divine permission is not God ignoring sin but his wise, purposeful ordering within providence. He is never evil's author; nothing sinful escapes his plan. Good and evil are governed differently, both under his sovereign rule.

items.title: Election and Reprobation
items.summary: Election is God's gracious choice of certain sinners in Christ for eternal life. Reprobation is his just passing over and condemning of the guilty, not the innocent. Reformed theology distinguishes withholding mercy from punishing unjustly.

items.title: Is Predestination Fair?
items.summary: Paul in Romans 9 denies that mercy and hardening make God unjust. Salvation rests on God's free prerogative, not human merit or foreseen faith. Human fairness does not judge the Creator; election and reprobation display his glory.

items.title: The Order of the Decrees
items.summary: Supralapsarians order election and reprobation logically before the decree to create and permit the fall; infralapsarians place election after creation and fall toward guilty sinners. Both affirm sovereignty and grace; Dort favors election from a fallen race.

items.title: Amyraldianism
items.summary: Amyraldianism teaches Christ died for all hypothetically on condition of faith while maintaining particular election. Critics say this reverses classic Reformed decree order and weakens redemption's sure efficacy for the elect, resembling conditional universalism.

items.title: Middle Knowledge
items.summary: Middle knowledge holds God knows counterfactual free choices before decreeing which world to create. Reformed theology rejects this as granting creatures independence over God's will and grounding providence in libertarian freedom rather than sovereign decree.

items.title: Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God
items.summary: Divine election does not cancel evangelism but motivates it: God has elect among the nations and uses preaching to save them. Urgent witness, prayer for the lost, and trust that God draws sinners coexist with particular redemption.

items.title: Our Creator God
items.summary: The one true God made heaven, earth, and all creatures by his power and sustains them continuously. He lacks nothing and needs no human service; all life depends on him. Creation is distinct from God yet entirely under his rule.

items.title: Creation Ex Nihilo
items.summary: Creation ex nihilo means God brought the universe into being by his word without preexisting matter or struggle. Creator and creation are distinct substances, excluding pantheism, dualism, and deism. All existence depends absolutely on his transcendent will.

items.title: Creation Days
items.summary: Evangelicals dispute whether Genesis 1 days are literal twenty-four-hour periods, long ages, framework symbolism, or analogical divine workdays. Ordinary days align with evening-morning language, Sabbath pattern, and historic readings, implying recent creation and no pre-fall animal death.

items.title: Historical Adam
items.summary: Adam was a real historical man directly formed by God, ancestor of the human race. Universal sin, imputation, and Christ as second Adam require one original pair; symbolic or population-only Adam models conflict with Genesis genealogies and apostolic teaching.

items.title: The End for Which God Created the World
items.summary: God created the world chiefly to display his glory through creatures who know, fear, and praise him. His perfect fullness overflows outward in goodness; the cosmos exists for worship, not because the Creator lacked love or needed companions.

items.title: Angels
items.summary: Angels are created spirit persons, mighty yet not divine, who serve God's purposes in revelation, protection, and judgment. Holy angels obey God; fallen angels rebel permanently. Scripture names orders such as cherubim, seraphim, and archangels without encouraging speculative obsession.

items.title: Demons
items.summary: Demons are fallen angels led by Satan who oppose God and assault believers through deception and accusation. Spiritual evil stands behind earthly darkness; Christ has defeated the devil. Christians resist in gospel truth without inventing elaborate demonologies or fear-driven speculation.

items.title: Providence
items.summary: Providence is God's continuous governance of all creatures—sustaining, directing, and governing every event toward his wise ends. He is not sin's author; nothing occurs outside his purpose. Creation receives fatherly care in prosperity and hardship alike.

items.title: Miracles
items.summary: Miracles are God's extraordinary works interrupting nature's usual course to authenticate redemptive revelation. They cluster around covenant milestones, Christ, and the apostles. Christian faith rests especially on the historical resurrection of Jesus as central sign.

items.title: Prayer
items.summary: Prayer is worshipful conversation in which God sovereignly chooses to accomplish his will partly through believers' requests. He commands asking in Christ's name with reverence, humility, and confident trust in the Father's goodness, not reluctance or unbelief.

items.title: Created Being and Crowning Achievement
items.summary: Humanity is finite creature, not deity, yet the apex of creation—crowned with glory and given dominion. Scripture centers history on image-bearing persons who steward, cultivate, and beautify the world rather than treating nature as ultimate or humanity as mere pollution.

items.title: Man as Body and Soul
items.summary: The human person unites body and soul as one living whole; death temporarily separates believer from body pending resurrection. Classical Christian anthropology prefers body-soul dichotomy over separate spirit-soul divisions, insisting both inner and outer life matter before God.

items.title: Where Do Our Souls Come From?
items.summary: Traducianism derives soul and body from parents, suiting inherited sin; creationism holds God directly creates each soul at conception, common in much Protestantism. Creationism helps explain Christ's sinless humanity without transmitting Adam's guilt through soul propagation.

items.title: Faculty Psychology
items.summary: Faculty psychology describes soul powers such as intellect, will, and affections. Reformed doctrine holds the fall corrupted every faculty, so salvation requires regenerating grace, not reason alone. Proper categories guard against intellectualism and undisciplined emotionalism.

items.title: Male and Female
items.summary: God created humanity as male and female, equally bearing his image yet physically and vocationally distinct. Sex is binary and purposeful in body, role, and relation; confusion in dress or behavior contradicts created nature and extends beyond marriage into all of life.

items.title: Marriage
items.summary: Marriage is a monogamous covenant between one man and one woman uniting as one flesh, promising fidelity, and ordinarily welcoming children. Ephesians presents it as a mystery picturing Christ and the church through complementarian husband and wife roles grounded in creation.

items.title: Transgenderism
items.summary: Scripture treats biological sex as God's fixed gift; identity and conduct must align with male or female creation, not inner feelings alone. Christians show compassion toward gender distress while rejecting ideologies that override God's word on body, dress, and sexual boundaries.

items.title: Image of God
items.summary: The image of God marks every human with dignity and moral responsibility, rooted in creation and retained after the fall. Christ perfectly displays God's image; redeemed believers are being renewed into his likeness, defining the worth of life and Christian hope.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Be Made in the Image of God?
items.summary: The image of God is humanity's created likeness to God in rational, moral, and relational capacities: representing his rule, seeking fellowship with him, and bearing knowledge, holiness, and righteousness. Sin defaces it; Christ restores image-bearers through the gospel.

items.title: What Are the Implications of Being Made in the Image of God?
items.summary: Bearing God's image confers innate dignity on every person, grounding respect for life across age, ability, and race. Humanity's proper end is knowing and obeying the Creator. Christ, as God's visible image, is the only right object of worship.

items.title: The Essence of Sin
items.summary: Sin is lawless rebellion against God: inherited depravity and voluntary transgression that exchanges the Creator for idols and cravings. It is moral guilt before a holy God, not mere imperfection, and demands grace.

items.title: The Origin of Sin
items.summary: Adam's first disobedience brought death, curse, and broken relationships into creation. Original sin denotes the corrupt nature transmitted from Adam; actual sins are our own deeds. All stand guilty from birth and need mercy outside themselves.

items.title: The Transmission of Sin
items.summary: Sin reaches all humanity through union with Adam as covenant head: his guilt and death are imputed to the race, as Christ's obedience brings life to those united to him. Faith transfers believers from Adam's condemnation to justification in the last Adam.

items.title: Total Inability
items.summary: Total depravity means sin corrupts every faculty; total inability means the fallen will cannot turn to God or merit salvation apart from regenerating grace. Spiritual death leaves humans hostile to God's law until the Spirit effectually draws them to Christ.

items.title: Human Nature in Its Fourfold State
items.summary: Reformed anthropology distinguishes four states: able to sin in innocency; unable not to sin in nature; able not to sin in grace through regeneration; unable to sin in glory. The redeemed will be perfected beyond Eden's probation.

items.title: Is Every Sin the Same in God’s Eyes?
items.summary: Every sin deserves eternal judgment, yet God distinguishes degrees of guilt. Scripture assigns varying penalties, weighs deliberate sin more heavily, and holds leaders accountable differently. Equal damnation does not erase real difference among offenses.

items.title: Sins Made More Heinous
items.summary: Aggravating factors increase sin's guilt: the sinner's office or knowledge, the victim offended, clear commands violated, repetition, timing during worship, and hardened conscience. Westminster theology uses these distinctions for discipline, warning, and counsel without equating all failures with high-handed rebellion.

items.title: Concupiscence
items.summary: Concupiscence is indwelling sinful desire remaining in believers after pardon. Reformed theology treats disordered inclinations themselves as sin, not merely neutral temptation until consent. Such corruption is mortified through confession, grace, and progressive sanctification until glorification.

items.title: Temptation
items.summary: Temptation denotes either divinely permitted testing or inward enticement from corrupt desire. External trials may be resisted without sin; evil lusts already signal indwelling corruption. Christ endured real testing without sinful longing; believers must resist before consent and outward act.

items.title: What Difference Does the Doctrine of Sin Make?
items.summary: The doctrine of sin grounds realistic expectations about human institutions and self-knowledge, keeps the gospel central for actual sinners in mission, and magnifies gratitude because every believer's conversion is wholly a work of grace.

items.title: Centrality of Covenant
items.summary: Covenant is Scripture's dominant framework for God's dealings with humanity, from creation to consummation. It organizes redemption through successive administrations, Christ's priestly work, and human mutual obligations. Reading the whole Bible covenantally reveals how grace unfolds through promised bonds.

items.title: Definition of Covenant
items.summary: A biblical covenant is God's solemn bond with his people, pledging blessings and stipulating obedience under sworn terms, penalties, witnesses, and signs. God initiates, defines conditions, and seals the relationship publicly rather than relating through vague sentiment.

items.title: Berith and Diatheke
items.summary: Hebrew berith and Greek diatheke both designate covenant. New Testament testament language in Hebrews reflects covenant ratification by blood and self-maledictory oath at the ceremony's start, not primarily modern wills activated only by death at the end.

items.title: Worship as Covenant Renewal
items.summary: Covenant worship follows a pattern of approach, proclamation of stipulations, blood sacrifice, congregational pledge, and fellowship meal in God's presence. Christian gathering echoes this rhythm through the Word, trust in Christ's blood, and the Lord's Supper as covenant remembrance.

items.title: Covenant of Redemption
items.summary: The covenant of redemption is the eternal pact between Father and Son to redeem the elect through the Son's obedience and sacrifice, applied by the Spirit. Salvation in history flows from this pre-creation agreement within one divine will.

items.title: Covenant of Works
items.summary: The covenant of works was God's arrangement with Adam as federal head: confirmed obedience would secure life; breach brought death on himself and posterity. Eden's elements parallel later covenants, making Adam's failure the counterpart to Christ's covenant obedience.

items.title: Covenant of Grace
items.summary: The covenant of grace promises salvation through Christ to sinners who receive it by faith alone, after the fall made the covenant of works impossible to keep. Its administrations differ from Adam to the church age, but one gracious promise unites the people of God.

items.title: The Noahic Covenant
items.summary: The Noahic covenant is God's universal, bloodless pledge after the flood to sustain seasons and refrain from another worldwide deluge, marked by the rainbow. It is common grace preserving a fallen world so redemptive covenant promises may unfold toward gospel fulfillment.

items.title: Abrahamic Covenant
items.summary: The Abrahamic covenant is God's gracious election of Abram and promise of nation, land, blessing, and worldwide redemption through his seed. It was ratified by oath and sacrifice; circumcision marked the line; fulfillment centers in Christ, blessing all nations by faith.

items.title: Mosaic Covenant
items.summary: The Mosaic covenant bound Israel to blessings and curses under law while administering grace through sacrifice and typology. It exposed sin, tutored faith, and governed national holiness without replacing Abrahamic promise or offering a separate merit path to eternal life.

items.title: Republication
items.summary: Republication holds the Mosaic covenant re-stated Adam's works principle for Israel as typological Adam, especially in do-and-live passages, while others insist Moses administers grace and Paul targets legalistic abuse. The debate shapes how obedience relates to justification and the law's Christian use.

items.title: Davidic Covenant
items.summary: The Davidic covenant promises an everlasting dynasty, royal sonship, rest, and a kingdom through David's offspring. Partial fulfillment came in Solomon; ultimate fulfillment is Christ the Messiah-King, through whom God concentrates Abrahamic and Mosaic hopes into eternal reign and salvation.

items.title: New Covenant
items.summary: The new covenant fulfills Jeremiah's promise of forgiven sin, inward law, and personal knowledge of God for Israel and believers united to Christ. It intensifies the covenant of grace beyond Mosaic failure; complete realization awaits glory when mediation ceases.

items.title: The Fathers Have Eaten Sour Grapes
items.summary: Jeremiah and Ezekiel reject the proverb that children suffer solely for ancestral sin. Generational effects exist, yet each person answers to God for personal rebellion. Exile judgment fell on Judah's own guilt, not innocent scapegoating; the new covenant aims at forgiven, accountable obedience.

items.title: The Newness of the New Covenant
items.summary: The new covenant is God's definitive arrangement in Christ, surpassing Moses while fulfilling prior promises. It grants clearer revelation, lasting grace, adopted sonship, and inclusion of all nations; outward participation without faith still excludes one from its saving benefits.

items.title: The Law and the Christian
items.summary: Christians are freed from the law's curse and from earning righteousness by works, yet God's moral commands remain binding. Ceremonial and civil statutes of Moses have reached their goal in Christ; Scripture still guides believers when interpreted through the Messiah.

items.title: Threefold Division of the Law
items.summary: Reformed theology divides Mosaic law into moral, ceremonial, and civil categories. The moral law, epitomized in the Ten Commandments, binds conscience universally; ceremonial rules foreshadowed Christ and expired in him; civil statutes governed national Israel.

items.title: Dispensationalism
items.summary: Dispensationalism reads Scripture through distinct eras of divine administration and often reserves future earthly promises for ethnic Israel apart from the church. Covenant theology sees one people of God in Christ, with Gentile believers grafted into Israel's covenant hope.

items.title: Baptist Covenant Theology
items.summary: Baptist covenant theology affirms one covenant of grace fulfilled in Christ while differing from Presbyterianism on baptism and church order. Earlier covenants typify grace, but only the new covenant administers its blessings to those united to Christ.

items.title: The Israel of God
items.summary: The Israel of God comprises all who trust Jesus as Messiah, not ethnic descent alone. Reformed teaching reconstitutes Israel around its king; New Testament writers apply Israel's covenant titles and privileges to the multinational church in him.

items.title: Logos
items.summary: Logos is John's name for the preexistent divine Word, eternally with the Father and fully God, through whom all things were made. The Word is personally distinct from the Father yet shares his nature; he is not a creature or lesser deity.

items.title: Virgin Birth
items.summary: The virgin birth is Mary's conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit without a human father. It secures his true humanity from her line and freedom from Adam's guilt, qualifying him as fully human and sinless redeemer.

items.title: Messianic Prophecies
items.summary: Messianic prophecies are Old Testament anticipations of a Davidic king and suffering servant fulfilled in Jesus. Gospel writers present his life as Israel's story perfected, showing Christ as the goal of prophetic patterns rather than arbitrary prooftexts.

items.title: Names and Titles of Jesus
items.summary: Jesus' names and titles declare his saving office: Christ as anointed King, Son of God as unique divine Son, Son of Man as Daniel's exalted figure, Lord as sovereign ruler, alongside explicit New Testament affirmations of his deity.

items.title: Jesus’s Witness to Himself
items.summary: Jesus' self-testimony, especially in John, presents him as bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, and vine, using divine I-am language. He claims eternal self-existence and demands trust in himself alongside the Father to know God.

items.title: Autotheos
items.summary: Autotheos means the Son possesses divine life and essence in his own right, not as a secondary god receiving deity from above. He shares the Father's life-giving power and judging authority while eternally proceeding from the Father.

items.title: Deity of Christ
items.summary: The deity of Christ is the doctrine that Jesus is fully God: preexistent, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, unchanging, and worthy of worship. New Testament witness ascribes to him every attribute and prerogative proper to the one God.

items.title: Humanity of Christ
items.summary: The humanity of Christ is true human body, soul, growth, fatigue, emotion, temptation, and death without sin. The Son became man to represent sinners, break death's dominion, and act as merciful high priest who atones for his people.

items.title: Eternal Sonship
items.summary: Eternal sonship teaches the Son had no beginning and always existed as God's Son, sharing the Father's essence. Denying his eternity makes the Father not eternally Father and leaves redemption without a Savior who is fully divine.

items.title: Incarnation
items.summary: The incarnation is the eternal Son's assumption of a real human nature in the one person Jesus Christ. He remained fully divine while adding humanity without change to his deity; from conception one person bears both natures.

items.title: Hypostatic Union
items.summary: The hypostatic union is the union of complete divine and human natures in one person, Jesus Christ. He has a single self, not two persons; human nature subsists in the Logos and was never an independent human individual apart from the Son.

items.title: Communicatio Idiomatum
items.summary: Communicatio idiomatum is the rule that what belongs to either of Christ's natures may be spoken of the one person. Properties are not mixed across natures, yet we may say God died on the cross meaning the incarnate Son, not the Father.

items.title: How Do the Two Natures Relate to Each Other?
items.summary: Reformed Christology holds that union with the Logos honored Christ's humanity and granted Spirit-given capacity without transferring divine attributes into the flesh. Each nature keeps its own properties; his body stayed localized and his human mind finite.

items.title: The Extra Calvinisticum
items.summary: The extra Calvinisticum teaches the Son's divine nature is united to humanity yet not enclosed within it; the Logos remained omnipresent while walking on earth. This safeguards limitless deity and a truly localized human body in the God-man.

items.title: Christological Heresies
items.summary: Christological heresies distort the apostolic confession of Christ's person: errors such as adoptionism, modalism, Ebionism, monophysitism, and monothelitism deny full deity, full humanity, or the unity of two natures and wills in one Savior.

items.title: Arianism
items.summary: Arianism taught the Son is the greatest creature, begotten in time, not of the Father's essence. The Council of Nicaea affirmed homoousios: the Son is same substance with the Father, eternally begotten, not made.

items.title: Docetism
items.summary: Docetism held Christ only seemed human and could not truly suffer; Apollinarianism replaced his human soul with the Logos. Orthodoxy requires a complete human nature for salvation—the Word assumed a whole man, not flesh without a human mind.

items.title: Nestorianism
items.summary: Nestorianism treated Christ's natures as parallel persons, denying Mary bore the unified God-man. Orthodoxy confesses one self-conscious subject in two natures: she bore the single person who is simultaneously God and man.

items.title: Eutychianism
items.summary: Eutychianism, or monophysitism, asserted one blended nature after the incarnation, dissolving true humanity. Chalcedon rejected this, insisting two unconfused natures remain in one person so Christ truly shares our substance.

items.title: Chalcedonian Definition
items.summary: The Chalcedonian Definition confesses one Lord Jesus Christ in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, change, division, or separation. He is complete in Godhead and manhood, one person, same essence as the Father in deity and as us in humanity.

items.title: “Whatever Is Not Assumed Cannot Be Healed”
items.summary: Chalcedon's Definition affirms one person in two natures, truly God and truly human. Gregory's principle: whatever humanity the Savior did not take cannot be redeemed. Full deity bridges us to God; full humanity heals our nature.

items.title: Christ’s Divine Self-Consciousness
items.summary: Jesus possessed steady self-knowledge as Messiah and Son of God, alongside genuine human growth in wisdom. One person united divine omniscience with a human mind that learned and lacked knowledge the Father had not revealed.

items.title: Kenosis
items.summary: Kenosis names the Son's voluntary humility in incarnation: not surrendering deity or divine attributes, but relinquishing divine privileges and glory to take servant form and die. Emptying means adding humanity, not subtracting divinity.

items.title: Spirit Christology
items.summary: Spirit Christology emphasizes the Holy Spirit's role in conceiving, anointing, empowering, and leading Christ's ministry. Correctly stressed, it upholds real humanity; wrongly stressed, it reduces miracles to prophetic empowerment and obscures the Son's own deity required for redemption.

items.title: Impeccability
items.summary: Impeccability holds that Christ was sinless and unable to sin. Temptation was real yet never arose from corrupt nature; his human will aligned with divine holiness. Genuine temptation does not require capacity to fall.

items.title: Two States
items.summary: Reformed theology divides Christ's mediatorial work into humiliation and exaltation. Humiliation veils glory, assumes flesh, and submits to law's demands and curse through suffering, death, and burial. Exaltation brings resurrection, ascension, session, and promised return.

items.title: Incarnation and Suffering
items.summary: The incarnation belongs to Christ's humiliation because the Son entered poverty, weakness, hidden deity, and lifelong suffering under a sin-cursed law. He bore bodily pain and soul anguish, including wrath against sin, to redeem ruined humanity.

items.title: Cry of Dereliction
items.summary: The cry of dereliction records Christ's real agony and curse borne for sinners while trusting the Father. Reformed teaching denies Trinitarian rupture: the Father's love continued, yet the Son experienced withdrawal of comfort and judicial wrath in his humanity.

items.title: Death and Burial
items.summary: Death and burial confirm Christ truly died under humiliation: betrayal, shame, mockery, and curse like sinners. His body removed from sight completes the path from hidden sorrows through Gethsemane and the cross, entering death's domain for believers' deliverance.

items.title: Descent into Hell
items.summary: Descent into hell in the creed often receives a non-literal Reformed reading: not a post-crucifixion journey to Hades, but summary of soul-agony Christ already endured, especially on the cross, by which he delivers believers from hell's torment.

items.title: Resurrection
items.summary: Resurrection marks humiliation's end and exaltation's start. Christ rose by Trinitarian power into an incorruptible, eternal body as firstfruits of believers, the life-giving Spirit. Death could not retain one whose sin-debt was fully paid; rising proves atonement accepted.

items.title: Ascension
items.summary: Ascension is Christ's bodily departure to heaven as he will return visibly. It confirms resurrection victory and bestows present blessings: spiritual gifts, heavenly intercession, universal lordship, and the Spirit because the Son went to the Father.

items.title: Session
items.summary: Session denotes Christ enthroned at God's right hand, inaugurating mediatorial kingship after completing obedience unto death. Figurative seatedness signals rest after finished satisfaction. All authority is his while he rules, intercedes, and advocates for his people.

items.title: Return
items.summary: The return is Christ's future visible, bodily coming as King and Judge, paralleling ascension. Exaltation includes resurrection, ascension, session, and this final vindication. Judgment belongs to the Son whom sinners rejected as mediator.

items.title: Prophet
items.summary: Christ as prophet speaks God's word with final authority, being revelation himself rather than merely receiving it. Anointed beyond measure by the Spirit, he discloses the Father's whole will through his ministry, Scripture, and the Spirit's work in the church.

items.title: Priest
items.summary: Christ's priesthood after Melchizedek's order surpasses Aaron through once-for-all atonement and ongoing heavenly intercession. Finished sacrifice on earth grounds present advocacy, sympathy with weakness, and silencing accusation so believers share heavenly life rather than repeating earthly sufferings.

items.title: King
items.summary: Christ as King alone heads the church, governing the elect, preserving his people, and executing judgment on rebels. Kingdom and church differ yet unite: the church displays kingdom life on earth as heaven's embassy until his reign fills all things.

items.title: Christ’s Kingdom
items.summary: Christ's kingdom appears as power over all creation, grace over the redeemed church, and future glory in the age to come—one reign in three expressions. Prayer for God's kingdom chiefly seeks gospel advance and pure worship, with universal rule serving those ends.

items.title: Introducing the Atonement
items.summary: The atonement is Christ's priestly work at the gospel's center: God objectively dealt with sin before applying forgiveness through faith. It includes active obedience to the law and passive bearing of its curse, motivated by love, justice, and divine pleasure united.

items.title: The Necessity of the Atonement
items.summary: Necessity of the atonement debates whether the cross was optional, decree-relative, or absolutely required. Reformed teaching commonly affirms absolute necessity: God's holiness, guilt, and stable moral law require penal satisfaction, which wrath and mercy meet at Calvary without dividing the Trinity.

items.title: The Perfection of the Atonement
items.summary: Perfection of the atonement means Christ's sacrifice is complete, unrepeatable, and sufficient; no creature adds merit. Pauline language about afflictions lacking refers to missionary suffering in proclaiming the gospel, not deficient redemption. Believers herald Christ; they never supplement his spotless offering.

items.title: Theories of the Atonement 1
items.summary: Historic atonement models each capture partial truth: recapitulation, ransom-to-Satan, commercial theory, moral influence, example, and Socinian denial of real guilt. None alone accounts for divine wrath and penal payment; penal substitution integrates what they grasp.

items.title: Theories of the Atonement 2
items.summary: Further atonement models include governmental, mystical, moral, vicarious repentance, and Barthian universalist tendencies, each weakening vicarious penalty or guilt. Penal substitution holds Christ stood in the believer's place to satisfy God's prescriptive and penal justice at the cross's heart.

items.title: Obedience and Conquest
items.summary: Atonement is manifold: Reformed teaching credits lifelong righteous obedience imputed to believers as second Adam, alongside Christus Victor's defeat of sin, death, and Satan. Substitution must not be replaced by conquest; both flow from one saving work.

items.title: Reconciliation and Redemption
items.summary: Atonement brings at-one-ment: God reconciles enemies by not counting sins against those in Christ, removing barriers on humanity's side at real cost. Redemption purchases deliverance from sin's slavery through Christ's blood, grounding forgiveness and hope.

items.title: Sacrifice and Satisfaction
items.summary: Sacrifice and satisfaction are cultic dimensions of atonement fulfilled in Christ as final high priest offering himself without blemish as substitute under curse. His death satisfies divine justice; because payment is complete, God justly forgives and cleanses sinners.

items.title: Expiation and Propitiation
items.summary: Expiation cleanses sin's guilt and defilement from offenders. Propitiation satisfies God's righteous wrath toward sin through Christ's sacrifice, reconciling sinners to him. Both dimensions of the cross belong together in atonement theology.

items.title: Limited Atonement
items.summary: Limited atonement holds Christ's death sufficient for all yet designed to redeem the elect effectively. He died as substitute for his people, securing actual salvation rather than only making redemption possible for everyone without exception.

items.title: Dort and Definite Atonement
items.summary: Definite atonement teaches that God purposed Christ's death to infallibly save the elect. The Synod of Dort affirmed sufficiency for all while holding the cross actually secured redemption for those given to Christ, not bare potential for all.

items.title: Crushed for Our Iniquities
items.summary: Isaiah's suffering servant was crushed by divine will to bear others' iniquities. God placed penal judgment on Christ by design so guilty sinners escape deserved wrath and gain the fruits of substitute obedience.

items.title: Ordo Salutis
items.summary: Ordo salutis names the logical sequence of salvation from God's eternal plan through calling, regeneration, faith, justification, sanctification, and glorification. It distinguishes divine monergistic acts from human responses without treating grace as a mechanical checklist.

items.title: The Work of the Holy Spirit 1
items.summary: The Holy Spirit applies Christ's accomplished redemption by convicting sin, regenerating hearts, granting understanding of truth, and assuring believers. His office unites the elect to Christ and exalts the Son rather than competing with him.

items.title: The Work of the Holy Spirit 2
items.summary: The Spirit sanctifies believers, distributes gifts for the church's edification, and seals every Christian at conversion. That seal marks God's ownership, authenticates true faith, and guarantees the promised inheritance as a down payment.

items.title: Union with Christ
items.summary: Union with Christ is the relational bond underlying every salvation blessing. Believers are in Christ, sharing his death and risen life, so election, justification, sanctification, and glory all flow from being joined to him.

items.title: General Calling
items.summary: General calling is the outward gospel invitation preached to all hearers, sincerely offering forgiveness and eternal life. It is external and universal in proclamation, even when God's secret purpose saves only those who believe.

items.title: Effectual Calling
items.summary: Effectual calling is God's successful inward call whereby the Spirit unites a sinner to Christ, renews the mind and will, and produces saving faith. It accompanies regeneration and transfers one from darkness into fellowship with Jesus.

items.title: Irresistible Grace
items.summary: Irresistible grace means that when God intends to convert a person, his regenerating call inevitably succeeds. Fallen humans cannot produce saving faith alone; the Spirit penetrates hardened hearts so divine purpose is not finally thwarted.

items.title: Regeneration
items.summary: Regeneration is the Spirit's supernatural new birth that imparts spiritual life where there was death at the outset of Christian existence. It precedes and enables faith and is distinct from, though related to, lifelong sanctifying renewal.

items.title: Monergism
items.summary: Monergism teaches regeneration as God's sole work without cooperation from the spiritually dead. New life precedes faith; the renewed will genuinely chooses God only because grace has already quickened and redirected the heart.

items.title: Conversion
items.summary: Conversion is the sinner's active turning from sin toward God that follows regeneration. It pairs repentance and faith and may be dramatic or gradual, distinguished from hollow profession or national reform lacking enduring obedience.

items.title: Repentance
items.summary: Repentance is Spirit-given sorrow for sin and deliberate turning from it toward God, joined with trust in Christ's mercy. It initiates at conversion and continues throughout the Christian life as ongoing reorientation to holiness.

items.title: Faith
items.summary: Saving faith is personal trust in Christ for redemption, not mere intellectual agreement. Wrought through election and regeneration yet commanded of sinners, it receives Christ alone and differs from temporary or merely historical belief.

items.title: Acts of Faith
items.summary: Classic Reformed faith comprises knowledge of gospel truth, assent to its reliability, and reliance on Christ's merit alone. Christian affections and obedience follow faith but are not definitional elements of justifying trust.

items.title: Faith and Assurance
items.summary: Assurance is confident knowledge that God accepts the believer in Christ, central to Reformation piety. It rests on divine promises, the Spirit's witness, and evident grace, though subjective certainty may fluctuate without canceling justification.

items.title: Justification
items.summary: Justification is God's forensic declaration that a guilty sinner is righteous in Christ. Through imputed obedience and remitted guilt, believers receive forgiven standing and heir status before God's law, grounded in Christ's perfect record.

items.title: Imputation
items.summary: Imputation is God's legal crediting of Christ's righteousness to believers and of their guilt to Christ. Justification depends on counted merit received by faith, not on incomplete internal holiness as the ground of divine acceptance.

items.title: Sola Fide
items.summary: Sola fide asserts justification through faith alone apart from works because faith receives Christ's righteousness rather than contributing merit. Standing before God rests on the Savior's obedience grasped by trust, not human achievement mixed in.

items.title: Does James Contradict Paul?
items.summary: Paul and James confront different problems: Paul rejects works of law as basis for divine verdict; James rejects inactive faith as genuine. Paul declares righteousness before God; James shows living faith vindicated before human observation.

items.title: Should We Take a “New Perspective” on Paul?
items.summary: The New Perspective interprets Paul chiefly as debating covenant boundary markers and ethnic identity, not personal guilt before God. Reformed critics welcome contextual correction but reject readings that undermine imputed righteousness and faith apart from works.

items.title: Time and Adjuncts
items.summary: Reformed theology locates justification at the historical moment of saving faith, not only in eternity's decree. Believers receive one full equal standing, without repeated verdicts, and that status remains despite subsequent sin and ongoing sanctification.

items.title: Adoption
items.summary: Adoption is God's gracious act making justified sinners his children for Christ's sake. It confers familial status, sonship privileges, bold prayer access, and eternal inheritance alongside Christ, the natural Son who opens the way.

items.title: How Does Sanctification Differ from Justification?
items.summary: Justification is an instantaneous forensic verdict removing guilt; sanctification is progressive moral renewal into Christ's image. The former is complete in status at faith; the latter grows by degrees and must not be confused with grounds of acceptance.

items.title: Three Uses of the Law
items.summary: God's moral law serves three purposes: it exposes sin and leads sinners to Christ, restrains evil in society, and guides believers in grateful obedience. Christians are freed from the law's curse yet still keep its commands as the rule of thankful life.

items.title: Trusting and Trying
items.summary: Sanctification requires active effort alongside faith, not passive surrender alone. Justification is by faith apart from works, but believers must mortify sin, pursue holiness, and strive toward godliness. Grace precedes duty and enables the moral struggle that true faith produces.

items.title: Good Works and Salvation
items.summary: Good works cannot merit salvation, yet they are required on the path God uses to bring believers to glory. They follow justification as fruit and evidence, express progressive holiness, and relate to final glory—all as gifts of grace, not earned wages.

items.title: Good Works and the Believer
items.summary: Believers cannot obey with legal perfection while sin remains, yet works done from faith for God's glory can please him. God accepts imperfect obedience in Christ and may reward sincere service. Christians can do genuine good, contrary to views that deny any righteous deeds.

items.title: Good Works and Merit
items.summary: Merit means a work so perfect that God must reward it. Reformed theology denies that human works merit eternal life: we already owe God all, our strength is grace, and our obedience is flawed. Good works remain necessary as evidence and path to glory by divine promise, not performance.

items.title: Perseverance
items.summary: Perseverance of the saints means true believers cannot lose salvation, yet apparent believers may prove they were never regenerate. God preserves the elect through faith, repentance, and the word's ongoing work. The doctrine encourages diligence, not presumptuous laxity.

items.title: Warning Passages
items.summary: New Testament warnings against falling away do not contradict election. God preserves his people through the means he appoints, including sober exhortations and threats. These passages are instruments the Spirit uses to keep believers watchful, complementing gospel promises rather than opposing them.

items.title: Glorification
items.summary: Glorification is the final stage of salvation in which God makes justified believers fully holy in body and soul. It completes adoption, conforms the redeemed to Christ's image, and brings the renewal of creation. Suffering, sin, and death end in the new creation.

items.title: Church
items.summary: The church is the assembly of people God calls out through Christ, rooted in biblical terms for gathered worship and covenant community. Scripture portrays it as Christ's body, building, and bride. Confessing the church belongs to Christian faith, not optional religious association.

items.title: Nature of the Church
items.summary: The church simultaneously exists as militant on earth and triumphant in heaven, visible in congregations yet defined by union with Christ, universal and local, organic and organized. Sound ecclesiology holds these paired truths together rather than collapsing one side into the other.

items.title: Unity
items.summary: Church unity is a mark of the true church: one Spirit joins believers to one Lord, one faith, and one baptism across nations. Many congregations need not destroy this unity. Genuine oneness requires shared apostolic doctrine, not indifference to error.

items.title: Holiness
items.summary: The church is holy positionally as Christ's set-apart body and temple, and she is called to grow in practical holiness. Visible failures do not revoke her sacred status. God guarantees the church will endure on earth until Christ completes her purification.

items.title: Catholicity
items.summary: Catholicity means the church is universal across time, place, and people, not identification with Rome. All nations share one apostolic faith. This mark resists ethnic exclusivism and nationalism that divide Christians who should stand united in gospel truth.

items.title: Apostolicity
items.summary: Apostolicity means the church remains faithful to the doctrine the apostles taught, not succession of bishops. God's people must guard and transmit the gospel of God, sin, Christ, and salvation by grace through faith. Churches are apostolic only as they proclaim that unchanged message.

items.title: Marks of the Church
items.summary: True churches are recognized chiefly by faithful preaching of God's word, rightly administered sacraments, and discipline. Pure scriptural teaching is essential; without it a gathering is not a church. Sacraments and discipline serve and protect the word rather than replace it.

items.title: Preaching
items.summary: Preaching is authoritative proclamation of God's word in worship, continuing the biblical pattern of heralds declaring divine truth. It is not mere discussion. Faithful exposition is a primary mark of Christ's church; without it a group lacks a defining feature of his assembly.

items.title: Members of the Church
items.summary: The invisible church comprises all the elect; the visible church consists of those who profess the true religion with their children. Adults enter by credible confession of faith; churches judge by outward profession and conduct. Covenant children belong to the visible community pending personal faith.

items.title: Church and State
items.summary: Church and state are distinct institutions with distinct ends and means. The church seeks spiritual eternal good through word and sacrament; the state maintains temporal peace and justice by the sword. Each has its own officers; neither should dominate the other.

items.title: Nature and Extent of Church Power
items.summary: Church power is ministerial and declarative: elders apply Scripture rather than legislate for conscience. It extends to doctrine, worship order, and member discipline, addressing souls spiritually without physical coercion. The church enforces Christ's law within these bounds.

items.title: Establishment Principle and Voluntary Principle
items.summary: The establishment principle favors state support and official recognition of true religion; the voluntary principle favors congregations formed and funded by free commitment without tax establishment. Reformed history debated both; voluntary association limits civil control over doctrine and church life.

items.title: Liberty of Conscience
items.summary: Liberty of conscience means only God rules the conscience through his word, not civil or ecclesiastical coercion of belief. It is not license for sin or rebellion. Churches must not bind beyond Scripture; states should respect sincere conviction while maintaining public order.

items.title: Regulative Principle
items.summary: The regulative principle holds that corporate worship must include only elements God has authorized in Scripture and exclude what he has not. Properly applied, it guards against human inventions in worship and frees congregations to worship with biblical confidence rather than cultural novelty.

items.title: Mission of the Church
items.summary: The church's institutional mission is to make disciples of all nations by baptizing and teaching obedience to Christ. This organized witness through the Spirit centers on proclamation, formation, and establishing churches—not every individual good work nor reduction to mere conversions alone.

items.title: Essential Reign and Mediatorial Reign
items.summary: Christ's essential kingship is his eternal divine rule over all creation. His mediatorial kingship is his gracious headship over the redeemed church as God-man. Creation serves the church's salvation; church and state therefore differ in how his lordship is expressed and extended.

items.title: Spirituality of the Church
items.summary: Spirituality of the church means the church's primary calling is spiritual and eternal under Christ's mediatorial headship, so ecclesiastical authority must not be confused with civil power. Church courts address church matters; ministers focus on salvation. The doctrine restrains clerical overreach without silencing biblical moral witness.

items.title: Creeds and Confessions
items.summary: Creeds and confessions are subordinate summaries of biblical doctrine for teaching, ordination, and unity. They do not replace Scripture but articulate orthodox faith the church has received. Confessing them joins local believers to the wider catholic church across history.

items.title: Gifts of the Spirit
items.summary: Spiritual gifts are abilities the triune God distributes to every believer for building up the church, not for personal prestige. Biblical lists illustrate rather than exhaust every grace; denying one's gift rejects the Spirit who equips the body for mutual service.

items.title: Miraculous Gifts
items.summary: Miraculous gifts are extraordinary abilities such as healing, tongues, and revelation. Continuationists expect them until Christ returns; cessationists hold they authenticated the apostolic foundation and ceased with it. Both affirm Scripture as final and the Spirit's ongoing work through the word.

items.title: Baptism in the Spirit
items.summary: Spirit baptism is the Spirit's work uniting every believer to Christ at conversion, not a second-tier experience for elites. Paul treats it as the common reality behind Pentecost, grounding unity amid diverse gifts within one body.

items.title: Filled with the Spirit
items.summary: Spirit-filling is living under the Holy Spirit's governing influence, producing self-control, Christlike character, worship, gratitude, and mutual submission. It contrasts with drunken excess and is pursued through prayer as believers mature in holiness.

items.title: Calling
items.summary: Effectual calling is God's summons of sinners to salvation, holiness, and glory in Christ. A call to pastoral ministry is discerned through desire, gifts, character confirmed by the church, and formal appointment—not through private mystical impressions alone.

items.title: Means of Grace
items.summary: Means of grace are the ordinary channels Christ instituted—especially preaching, sacraments, and prayer—through which the church receives saving and sanctifying grace when embraced with faith, not by empty ritual alone.

items.title: Semper Reformanda
items.summary: Semper reformanda means the church already confessed as Reformed must continually be shaped by Scripture in doctrine and life. The phrase describes passive submission to God's word, not license to revise faith to suit culture or progressive theology.

items.title: Sacraments
items.summary: Sacraments are holy ordinances Christ established: visible signs that represent, seal, and apply covenant blessings to believers through faith. They complement preaching by engaging sight, touch, taste, and smell without operating as automatic magic.

items.title: How Many Sacraments?
items.summary: A sacrament must be instituted by Christ and serve as an ordinary means of special grace. On that definition only baptism and the Lord's Supper qualify; rites such as confirmation, penance, orders, anointing, and marriage do not.

items.title: Baptism
items.summary: Baptism is Christ's initiatory rite in the triune name, marking entrance into covenant membership. Water signifies cleansing from sin and judgment; the sign visibly seals gospel promises for those united to Christ by faith without replacing faith itself.

items.title: Recipients of Baptism
items.summary: All who trust Christ should be baptized. Reformed Christians also baptize believers' children as covenant heirs, continuing the pattern in which Old Testament infants received the initiatory sign of belonging to God's people.

items.title: Mode of Baptism
items.summary: Baptism's essential meaning is union with Christ and washing from sin, not a required mode of immersion. Valid baptism applies water in the triune name; Scripture and narrative evidence allow pouring or sprinkling as well as immersion.

items.title: What Does Baptism Seal?
items.summary: Baptism seals covenant promises—membership, forgiveness, new life, and resurrection hope—not automatic regeneration. Faith remains indispensable; the sign marks privileges and obligations within God's family until personally embraced by trust in Christ.

items.title: Who Can Baptize?
items.summary: Baptism belongs to ordained gospel ministers who preach with authority and shepherd the visible church. Restricting administration to officers preserves the rite's seriousness and keeps initiation under accountable pastoral oversight.

items.title: How Many Times Should I Be Baptized?
items.summary: Baptism is administered once because initiation into Christ is unrepeatable. Reformed Christians recognize irregular yet valid baptisms with water in the triune name and gospel intent, without requiring rebaptism when converts come from defective communions.

items.title: The Lord’s Supper
items.summary: The Lord's Supper is Christ's covenant meal in which believers receive bread and wine as signs of his body and blood. It seals forgiveness, renews fellowship, strengthens faith, and proclaims his death until he returns.

items.title: Real Presence
items.summary: Real presence at the Supper denotes genuine communion with Christ, not agreement on mechanism. Reformed theology confesses a spiritual presence: the exalted Lord feeds believers by the Spirit through faith, without localizing his human nature in the elements.

items.title: A Table or an Altar?
items.summary: Protestants gather at a table to receive a completed sacrifice, not at an altar to re-offer Christ. The Supper memorializes and applies the once-for-all cross; sacramental language treats the elements as signs, not a repeated unbloody oblation.

items.title: Who Should Receive the Lord’s Supper?
items.summary: The Lord's Supper is for professing believers who examine themselves, remember Christ, and discern his body. It requires active faith and repentance, so it is not administered to infants, unlike baptism, which may be received passively as an entry sign.

items.title: Church Membership
items.summary: Church membership is formal commitment to a particular local congregation under recognized leaders. Scripture presents the church as an accountable body whose members vow mutual fellowship, service, and submission to shepherds who know and watch over their souls.

items.title: Church Discipline
items.summary: Church discipline is Christ's delegated authority to confront sin within the fellowship through escalating steps toward repentance or exclusion. Its aim is restoration and purity, treating unrepentant members as outsiders while hoping for their salvation.

items.title: Church Officers in the New Testament Church
items.summary: Ascended Christ gave officers to build his church. Apostles and prophets belonged to the foundational era with unique authority; the enduring gift is the pastor-teacher who shepherds and instructs the congregation in the ongoing ministry of the word.

items.title: The Work of Ministry
items.summary: The work of ministry centers on pastor-teachers whom Christ gave to equip saints, serve the church, and build up the body. Reformed exegesis stresses that faithful preaching is a primary bond of unity, not a secondary support for lay activity elsewhere.

items.title: How Many Offices in the Church?
items.summary: Reformed churches debate two offices—ruling elder and deacon—versus a distinct pastoral office. Biblical terms for elder, overseer, and pastor overlap; both schemes usually place teaching elders at the head of a shared eldership.

items.title: Elders
items.summary: Elders are qualified men appointed to teach and govern the local church with mature character and doctrinal competence. Their office combines spiritual oversight and public instruction, distinct from deacons who focus on practical mercy without required ruling authority.

items.title: Deacons
items.summary: Deacons are ordained servants who meet tangible needs—food, poverty, sickness, and vulnerability—alongside elders. They exemplify Christlike mercy ministry; most Reformed churches restrict the diaconate to qualified men while affirming women's many other ministries.

items.title: Divine Appointment for Church Government
items.summary: Presbyterian polity holds that the church, as God's kingdom by special divine institution, should receive its basic government from Scripture rather than human invention. That does not require every procedural detail to be specified in the Bible.

items.title: Who Governs the Church: The Pope?
items.summary: Roman Catholicism claims supreme church authority for the pope as Peter's successor. Reformed theology typically identifies the church's foundation as Peter's confession of Christ, not a permanent Petrine office transferring unique headship to Rome.

items.title: Who Governs the Church: The Bishops?
items.summary: Episcopal polity elevates bishops above elders with regional ordaining power. Reformed exegesis often treats elder and overseer as one office, with apostles holding temporary authority not modeled as a permanent tier above pastors.

items.title: Who Governs the Church: The Congregation?
items.summary: Congregationalism requires member consent on major decisions and independent local churches. Presbyterians affirm member involvement but assign binding keys-of-the-kingdom authority to ordained elders, not to the congregation as a whole for preaching and ordination.

items.title: Who Governs the Church: The Elders?
items.summary: Presbyterianism places Christ-delegated rule in session elders locally and in connectional courts regionally. Higher assemblies wield the same authority more widely, as in Acts 15, not a superior power distinct from local elders.

items.title: Decently and in Order
items.summary: Paul commanded worship and assembly to proceed decently and in order. Reformed churches treat structured process as biblical discipline against Corinthian disorder, not cold formalism incompatible with sincere devotion.

items.title: Death and Hell
items.summary: Death remains the last enemy for believers though it brings them to the Lord. Scripture uses terms for the grave, Sheol or Hades, and Gehenna for final fiery judgment upon the wicked.

items.title: Hell as Divine Punishment
items.summary: Hell is not mere self-chosen separation from God. Scripture portrays God actively executing stored wrath and destruction on the impenitent, a righteous divine punishment rather than solely passive absence of Christ.

items.title: Universalism
items.summary: Universalism teaches that all persons will eventually be saved. Reformed theology rejects this, reading cosmic reconciliation texts as Christ's universal lordship while retaining warnings of wrath and exclusion for unrepentant rebels.

items.title: Annihilationism
items.summary: Annihilationism holds the wicked are finally destroyed rather than eternally conscious in torment, sometimes called conditional immortality. Classic Reformed interpretation sees ongoing punitive existence in narrative and apocalyptic texts, not mere extinction.

items.title: Inclusivism
items.summary: Inclusivism allows salvific benefit through Christ for some without explicit faith, via sincerity or other religions. Exclusivism insists conscious trust in the Son is necessary, consistent with John's warnings that rejection stands condemned.

items.title: Do Believers Go to Heaven When They Die?
items.summary: Believers who die enter immediate fellowship with Christ while awaiting bodily resurrection and renewed creation. Paul treated death as gain; pastoral assurance for the dying need not exclude the eventual remaking of heaven and earth.

items.title: Intermediate State
items.summary: The intermediate state is the soul's condition between death and final resurrection. Reformed confessions teach perfected believers rest in glory with Christ, wicked souls in torment, rejecting purgatory and soul sleep.

items.title: Judgment according to Works
items.summary: Final judgment accounts for deeds in the body yet salvation remains by grace through faith. Works function as evidence of genuine faith; for believers the judgment seat displays fruit rather than merit for entry.

items.title: Heavenly Rewards
items.summary: Scripture teaches degrees of punishment; believers' varying heavenly rewards are debated. Some Reformed voices stress one inheritance in Christ; others read crown and loss language as differing rewards or warnings about empty Christian living.

items.title: What Will Heaven Be Like?
items.summary: Final heaven is God dwelling with a renewed creation, not disembodied spirits forever. Revelation envisions a holy city and new earth; saints reign with Christ in embodied joy surpassing earthly experience.

items.title: Partial Preterism
items.summary: Partial preterism locates much apocalyptic fulfillment in the first century, especially around AD 70, while still awaiting Christ's visible return, general resurrection, and new creation, unlike full preterism which places all prophecy in the past.

items.title: The Great Tribulation
items.summary: Tribulation names affliction Christians face throughout this age. Reformed eschatology rejects pretribulational rapture escape; God preserves his people in intensifying trial before Christ returns, as Revelation portrays saints enduring rather than evacuating.

Revelation's 144,000 symbolizes the entire redeemed people sealed by God, not a literal ethnic remnant. The figure combines tribes and apostles squared, expressing completeness; the stylized list serves theological rather than census purposes.

The beast's number 666 invites symbolic reading as human imperfection imitating divine completeness. Gematria identifications such as Nero remain speculative; Revelation pairs figurative beasts with figurative numbers rather than precise historical codes.

items.title: All Israel Will Be Saved
items.summary: Paul teaches God has not rejected ethnic Israel; a remnant remains elect by grace. All Israel will be saved means the full number of elect Jews ingrafted by faith, not universal future conversion of every ethnic Israelite.

items.title: Millennial Views
items.summary: Millennial views map Revelation twenty diversely: historic and dispensational premillennialism, amillennialism seeing the present church age symbolically, and postmillennialism expecting gospel triumph before Christ returns. They differ over timing, literalism, and Israel-church relations.

items.title: When Does the Millennium Take Place?
items.summary: Amillennialists often read Revelation twenty recapitulating earlier visions, placing the millennium in the present church age despite sequential wording. Binding Satan, saintly reign, and final judgment reappear under different symbols rather than strictly linear future stages.

items.title: What Is Meant by Satan Being Bound for a Thousand Years?
items.summary: Satan's millennial binding means Christ's cross victory restrains unified worldwide deception that would destroy the church, not Satan's total inactivity. Believers still wrestle with evil while nations cannot eliminate gospel witness entirely.

items.title: What Is Meant by the First Resurrection?
items.summary: The first resurrection in Revelation twenty denotes souls of martyrs and faithful dead reigning with Christ in heaven during the millennium, not a separate bodily resurrection before the general resurrection of all mankind.

items.title: The Glorious Appearing
items.summary: Christ's second coming will manifest open glory, power, and judgment unlike his first advent in humility. Revelation presents him as conquering King and Lamb; believers await visible return though its timing remains unknown.
